images.title: Where ideas take shape
images.caption: World Philosophy Day
images.desc: It's World Philosophy Day, when big thinkers gather to discuss life's eternal mysteries. To celebrate, today's image features the "Body of Knowledge" sculpture at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany, which molds steel letters from eight different alphabets into a human form. Spanish artist Jaume Plensa explains: "Our body is the home of the spirit. The place in which ideas live." On World Philosophy Day, we're all encouraged to look beyond easy answers and explore the questions that shape us, and the world around us.

images.title: Hunting from dusk till dawn
images.caption: A pair of barn owls at dusk
images.desc: These barn owls, bathed in evening light, are waiting for the hunt to begin. As night falls, these birds of prey swoop into action, listening for tiny movements in grass or leaves made by mice and voles. Their heart-shaped faces help funnel sound into some of the sharpest ears in the animal kingdom. This allows them to locate their prey with pinpoint precision in the dark before swooping silently, their soft feathers muffling their approach. In fall, young barn owls strike out to find their own territories. As the nights grow longer, you might spot them earlier in the evening, gliding over fields in search of dinner.

images.title: Step into the great outdoors
images.caption: Trail of the Cedars, Glacier National Park, Montana
images.desc: It's time to breathe in that crisp fall air and step into the great outdoors. Today's image features the Trail of the Cedars, part of more than 1,100 kilometres of hiking trails in Glacier National Park, Montana. Its 1.4-kilometre loop includes a raised boardwalk which cuts a path through western red cedars and hemlock trees. The park boasts routes for all abilities, taking in alpine lakes, wildflower meadows, mountain passes and wilderness stretching to the Canadian border.

images.copyright: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, New Mexico, USA (© Chiara Salvadori/Getty Images)
images.title: Built to last
images.caption: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument
images.desc: Incredible views and rock-solid foundations are part of the charm of these ancient dwellings, set into the cliffside in New Mexico. Nomads had long used the natural caves above Cliff Dweller Creek as temporary shelter, but it was the Native American Mogollon people who made them their home. Archaeologists believe they created dozens of rooms inside five alcoves in the 1270s and 1280s. Up to 15 families lived here at any one time, raising children, making pottery and overlooking the fertile Gila River valley where they grew crops and hunted wildlife. For reasons unknown, the Mogollon people moved on around 1300, leaving behind one of the American Southwest's most important archaeological sites.

images.copyright: Frozen azalea with red leaves (© avoferten/Shutterstock)
images.title: Frosty foliage
images.caption: Frost on azalea foliage
images.desc: As fall's first frost sets in, ice crystals form on the leaves of evergreen shrubs, like this azalea. Long gone are the pinks, oranges and yellows of their spring blooms, but a new colourful display awaits, as their green leaves turn shades of red and purple. For the plants, the new pigments protect their leaves as temperatures drop, but for gardeners, they create a vibrant fall display, framed in white frost. When spring arrives, new growth will restore the shrub's green leaves, and the colourful cycle begins anew.

images.title: The only way is up
images.caption: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
images.desc: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fuelling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upward, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 completed buildings at least 150 metres tall — more than any other city.

images.title: Hidden depths
images.caption: Ice on Abraham Lake in Alberta
images.desc: Dawn's first light is reflected on the frozen surface of Abraham Lake, framed by Rocky Mountains peaks. In winter, this picturesque lake in Alberta is famous for its frozen bubbles of methane gas, trapped beneath the ice. Strong winds keep the surface clear of snow, offering winter-long views. Come spring, when the ice thaws, the gas escapes into the atmosphere.

images.title: Architecture without an architect
images.caption: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah
images.desc: Just north of Moab, Utah, Arches National Park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches – the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.
